articles.title: Dodgers fan’s brutal response when entire stadium demanded he hand foul ball to young Braves fan
articles.summary: A viral video of a Los Angeles Dodgers fan refusing to give an NLDS foul ball to a young Atlanta Braves fan has sparked a massive online debate
articles.body:
Game 3 NLDS Bragging rights wasn't all that the Los Angeles Dodgers took from the Atlanta Braves on Tuesday night.

A Dodgers fan wearing a Yoshinobu Yamamoto jersey caught a foul ball during Tuesday night's game. A spectator seated nearby was taking a video of his excited reaction then said, "Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!"

The fan then looked at the camera, shrugged, and said, "I'm sorry, I can't! I'm not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid!"

The video then panned to the kid in question, who was wearing a Braves jersey and had a disappointed look on his face.

The camera then panned back to the Dodgers fan , who was gloating over his ball then posed for a photo with it.

The video has gone viral, with one X user who reposted it getting over 2.6 million views on about 12 hours. The original TikTok video also has nearly a million views.

It has sparked a debate about whether adult fans are obliged to give little kids balls that they catch at baseball games. Some believe an adult fan who caught a ball fair and square should not be shamed if they want to keep it, while others feel like an adult fan should be entitled to give their catch away to a fan.

This Dodgers fan was clearly in the former group.

articles.title: NFL Catchup: Eagles' Injuries Mount; Jayden Daniels Trending Toward Return
articles.summary: Here's the latest from around the NFL on Wednesday.
articles.body: Wednesday brought a full slate of injury news across the league as teams finalized their first reports of Week 5. Philadelphia's situation keeps growing, while there was better news in Washington and lingering uncertainty in Baltimore and Los Angeles. Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith both missed practice for the Eagles, adding to an already long injury list, but Jayden Daniels is trending toward his season return for the Commanders. Elsewhere, Lamar Jackson's Week 5 status remains up in the air for the Ravens, and the winless Chargers will likely be without right tackle Joe Alt against the Broncos. Here's the latest from around the NFL on Wednesday. Barkley, Smith Both Miss Practice Wednesday Philadelphia running back Saquon Barkley and wide receiver DeVonta Smith officially did not practice Wednesday, both sidelined by hamstring injuries as the Eagles begin preparations for Sunday's game against the Jaguars in London. Smith was already trending toward missing extended time after sitting out all of last week's practice and being ruled out against the Rams, and Wednesday's absence does little to change that outlook. Barkley, meanwhile, is considered week-to-week after the injury limited him to just four snaps in Sunday's loss, though he's believed to have avoided anything more serious. The two join an already lengthy Eagles injury list that includes tight end Dallas Goedert (knee), linebacker Zack Baun (concussion), cornerback Quinyon Mitchell (knee), plus guard Landon Dickerson and tight end Eli Stowers on injured reserve. Right tackle Lane Johnson's retirement earlier this week only adds to Philadelphia's depth concerns heading into the trip overseas. Jayden Daniels Returns To Practice, Set To Start Jayden Daniels could be back on the field for game action soon. The Commanders quarterback was a full participant in Wednesday's practice, putting him on track to start Sunday at home against the Giants three weeks after dislocating his left elbow against Dallas in Week 2 — the second such dislocation of his career. Daniels wore a brace on the elbow during practice that he'll continue wearing moving forward, embracing a new approach to protecting himself. "I'm going to embrace the brace," Daniels said. Coach Dan Quinn said the team has been working with Daniels on technique to avoid re-injury, comparing it to how a running back protects the ball. Daniels said he's still adjusting to playing with the brace. "Just trying to get used to it, it's kind of part of me now. ... I'm not really just thinking about it, I'm out there playing." Giants coach John Harbaugh said his team is preparing for Daniels to play, and edge rusher Abdul Carter said Washington's quarterback won't be eased into contact: "With the injury he has, we want him to run. We kind of encourage it, just to see how he reacts." Lamar Jackson Misses Practice, Status For Week 5 Uncertain Lamar Jackson sat out practice for the Ravens on Wednesday, three days after injuring his ankle in a win over Tennessee, and wasn't made available to speak. Jackson's ankle rolled under an opposing player late in the first half Sunday, and he didn't return to the game. Head coach Jesse Minter said there's still time for Jackson to prove he's ready. "There is a lot of time between now and Sunday. To Lamar's credit, he is getting a lot of treatment and doing things. There will be a point later in the week where we will figure out kind of where it is at," Minter told reporters, adding that Jackson has the experience to play without a full week of practice if it comes to that: "I think he's in that category, based on everything that he has accomplished." If Jackson can't go, Tyler Huntley, who led Baltimore to wins over Chicago and Green Bay last season, would start in place of Jackson. Several other Ravens also sat out Wednesday, including edge rusher Trey Hendrickson (finger), cornerback Marlon Humphrey (hamstring/calf), tackle Ronnie Stanley (toe/ankle) and guard Andrew Vorhees (foot), while tight end Durham Smythe (Achilles) was placed on injured reserve. Baltimore plays at Atlanta on Sunday night. Chargers RT Joe Alt Not Expected To Play Sunday The Chargers are winless through the first month of the NFL season, and they were just dealt some bad news. Right tackle Joe Alt is expected to miss the Chargers Week 5 matchup against the Broncos due to a neck injury he suffered during last week's loss to the Seahawks, according to NFL Network. The Notre Dame alum didn't practice Wednesday, and he is now reportedly expected to miss Sunday's game against the Broncos. The Chargers have no plans to place him on injured reserve despite the absence. Alt went down late in the first half with a neck injury and was replaced by Travis Burke. He was one of eight Chargers who sat out practice Wednesday, a sign the team is leaning toward resting him through the week rather than rushing him back for Sunday's matchup with Denver. articles.title: With A Taste Of Tequila, Papi Salutes Teoscar Hernandez And The Dodgers
articles.summary: MLB on FOX analyst David Ortiz didn't mind saluting Dodgers outfielder Teoscar Hernandez with a bit of tequila.
articles.body: The Los Angeles Dodgers are heading back to the NL Championship Series for the third straight season, and remain on course for a World Series three-peat. That's a cause for celebration in itself. Which is why MLB on FOX analyst David Ortiz didn't mind saluting Dodgers outfielder Teoscar Hernandez with a swig of tequila after the team eliminated the Atlanta Braves in Game 4 of the NL Division Series. Ortiz lauded Hernandez's ability to deliver for the Dodgers in crucial moments despite being on a team with more celebrated stars like Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts. "Every time you come out quietly and do some damage, brother. … You always come through when they really, really need you. You always prepare for those moments," Ortiz said. While Hernandez went hitless in Games 3 and 4 against the Braves, the 33-year-old outfielder had a crucial two-run home run in the 5-3 win in Game 1. Hernandez, as he was drenched with beer and champagne by his celebrating teammates in the visitors' locker room in Atlanta, said he thrives when the team needs him the most. "I love [the moments]. Throughout my career, I'm not afraid to fail. I think that's the key, and I try to pass that to thing to the new guys – don't be afraid to fail," Hernandez explained. "I just want to be that guy in that tough spot." Hernandez came on late toward the end of the season after struggling this summer. But things turned for him in September, where Hernández’s final month saw him hit .341 with a .965 OPS, along with four homers and 18 RBIs. When asked by MLB on FOX analyst Alex Rodriguez about the mid-season adjustments he made as a hitter, Hernandez credited his improvement at the plate to switching up his stance. "I had like three different stances that I used throughout the season and the way I'm hitting right now is one of them. I used to have a little bit of a leg kick. Another one is similar to Shohei, to stay on the ground. "And another is pulling my front leg outside and doing a toe tap. I do this to control my body, to see the ball traveling and use the whole field." Hernandez and the Dodgers will be back in action on Sunday in Game 1 of the NLCS on FOX.

articles.title: Un equipo de ingenieros marroquíes desarrolla un dron de ataque autónomo que navega sin GPS por satélite
articles.standfirst: Se ha diseñado con tecnología avanzada y un coste de 1,15 millones de dólares
articles.summary: Se ha diseñado con tecnología avanzada y un coste de 1,15 millones de dólares
articles.body: Cinco ingenieros marroquíes han construido un dron de ataque autónomo que es capaz de navegar sin GPS por satélite. Al no tener la ‘vulnerabilidad’ de estar localizado, constituye un avance para la tecnología al frente de batalla. Ha sido desarrollado por la startup de defensa Ballistic Defense System (BDS), que tiene sede en Rabat. Se llevó a cabo en menos de un año y medio, y la inversión ha sido de 1,15 millones de dólares aproximadamente, y financiación propia. Así lo recoge una información reciente publicada en el medio de comunicación Africa Business Insider. Muchos de los artilugios diseñados hasta el momento se controlaban a distancia. Pero, en este caso, los datos óptimos se procesan a través de un ordenador pequeño. Muy pequeño. Concretamente, del tamaño de una mano, pero que tiene la capacidad de controlar de alguna manera el diseño. Cuando ya está en la zona objetivo, son los propios sistemas, hechos con inteligencia artificial, los que van hasta el ataque final. Y lo hacen con bastante precisión, de apenas un metro, tal y como se ha comprobado en las pruebas que se han hecho recientemente en Europa. “Lo más difícil ha quedado atrás”, ha señalado el cofundador de BDS, Fahd Laamoumi, a Morocco World News, en las que hace un repaso de todo lo que han podido hacer hasta el momento con este avance. “La autonomía está al servicio de las decisiones humanas; no las sustituye”, ha añadido. “En materia de defensa, las afirmaciones no significan nada sin pruebas”, ha concretado. El sistema de navegación se validó a través de un diseño de unos 17 kilos a lo largo de 800 kilómetros de ensayos de vuelo en la localidad belga de Chimay. Pero quieren más. Quieren evaluar un modelo operativo más grande, que alcance los 250 kilos y tenga un alcance de 2.000 kilómetros.

articles.title: Dodgers And Brewers Advance, Yankees Are Out: 4 Takeaways From Division Series Slate
articles.summary: The Dodgers and Brewers are set for another collision course, while the Yankees simply imploded.
articles.body: The Dodgers and Brewers are set for another collision course, while the Yankees simply imploded. We're down to five teams left with World Series hopes. In the National League, we'll have a rematch of last year's NLCS. And in the American League, the Rays swept the Yankees and now await the winner of the White Sox-Guardians series for a chance at the World Series. Here are our takeaways from Wednesday's action: 1. Andy Pages Is Writing His Redemption Story Rowan Kavner: Before the National League Division Series shifted from Los Angeles to Atlanta, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts gave a vote of confidence to his struggling All-Star center fielder. After going 4-for-51 in the postseason during the Dodgers’ 2025 World Series run, Andy Pages started this October hitless in the first two games of the NLDS. He also was banished from using ABS challenges again after another failed attempt in a year full of them. But Roberts stuck by the 25-year-old outfielder, who was one of the Dodgers’ most productive players this season. "I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash," Roberts said. "I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team." Roberts just wanted to see better at-bats from the whiff-prone outfielder, who had struck out in half of his plate appearances over Games 1 and 2. The Dodgers’ manager didn’t have to wait long. Pages responded with two hits and a run scored in Game 3, then delivered a game-breaking, series-sealing, two-run knock in Wednesday’s Game 4 to send the Dodgers through to the National League Championship Series in a 4-1 win. "I've been preparing myself all series for a moment like that," Pages said. Braves starter Tyler Mahle gave the Dodgers’ lineup fits, just as he did to most of his opponents after getting dealt from San Francisco to Atlanta at the trade deadline. Mahle, who had a 5.13 ERA in 18 appearances with the Giants and a 1.99 ERA in nine second-half starts with the Braves, held the Phillies to one run in seven innings in the wild-card series and the Dodgers to one run through the first six innings Wednesday night. The only hit Mahle surrendered through his first four innings was a single to Pages in the third. Four innings later, the biggest moment of the game found Pages after reliever Didier Fuentes loaded the bases and Braves manager Walt Weiss called upon Robert Suarez with two outs and the bases loaded. The free-swinging center fielder demonstrated restraint, taking the first two pitches outside the zone. He worked a 3-1 count, fouled off a four-seamer down the middle and then delivered the blow to end the Braves’ season with a base hit back up the middle. It was the Dodgers’ only hit with a runner in scoring position during the series. They hit eight home runs over the four games, including three from Max Muncy, whose solo shot in the ninth inning of Game 4 gave Dodgers closer Edwin Diaz some extra insurance before he locked down his second straight save to send the Dodgers forward to the NLCS for the eighth time in the last 11 years. They’re one series away – a rematch with the Brewers in the NLCS – from a third straight trip to the World Series. 2. Yankees' Undoing? Losing Focus Deesha Thosar: If there’s any team to avoid making a mistake against, it’s the Rays. The Yankees know that. They learned that lesson the hard way during their atrocious, four-error performance in Game 2 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field. On Wednesday night in the Bronx, with their backs against the wall, the last thing they could afford to do was lose focus, or even get gassed. Yankees left-hander Max Fried appeared fatigued and wiped out on his final pitch of the night: a 77.9 mph sweeper that he could not have hung more if he tried. That was the dagger. Rays left fielder Victor Mesa Jr. promptly sent it to the moon, breaking up the tied game with a go-ahead, two-run rocket. It was Mesa’s first career postseason home run, and it gave the Rays a lead they would never relinquish. And that was how the Yankees season ended, by getting swept at the hands of their division rival. It’s a story we witnessed as recently as last year. It’s a problem the Yankees do not know how to fix. Tampa Bay defeated New York, 4-3, and advanced to the ALCS for the first time since 2020. The Rays will go up against the winner of the other ALDS matchup between the White Sox and Guardians, with Chicago owning a 2-1 edge in the series heading into Thursday’s Game 4. The Rays received offensive production from unsung heroes in their Game 3 clincher. Third baseman Junior Caminero was quiet — besides the throwing error he committed in the eighth inning. Yandy Diaz led off the game with a single, and then was sent down in each of his next three at-bats. Jonathan Aranda contributed with an RBI single in the third, but most of Tampa Bay’s damage came from their overlooked bench players. Right fielder Ryan Vilade, who posted a 108 OPS+ in 96 games for the Rays this year, tested Fried twice on Wednesday. In his first at-bat, Vilade sent a hard-hit fly ball to the warning track in left. In his second at-bat, he took Fried deep on a solo shot to the short porch in right field. Vilade’s fly ball to right field counted as a home run in exactly one major-league ballpark: Yankee Stadium. Wednesday was Vilade’s first career playoff game. His home run was his first career postseason hit. "It was pretty crazy," Vilade said. "Definitely didn't expect anything, like homer being your first postseason hit. You dream about it, and then to do it was really special. And I think, in the moment of the game, it was super cool as well. Just blessed." 3. MLB's Best Team Cools Down Its Hottest One Rowan Kavner: The questions entering October about whether a Milwaukee offense that led the majors in batting average and on-base percentage could successfully use that contact-heavy formula in the postseason, where home runs tend to rule, will have to be tabled for now. So far, so good. Hours after the White Sox lineup set a postseason record striking out 19 times, the Brewers punched their return ticket to the National League Championship Series showcasing the opposite approach Wednesday night, one that helped them win a franchise-record 103 games. In a 3-1 win in the deciding Game 4 of the National League Division Series, they did not strike out until their 29th batter of the game. By then, the Padres were already on their sixth pitcher of the night, Mason Miller, who was on the mound one day after celebrating the birth of his first child. This time, three days after suffering a blown save in a Game 2 defeat, the standout closer had no lead to protect. The Brewers brought San Diego to the brink despite the Padres scoring first in each of the first three games of the series. On Wednesday, they flipped that script when Sal Frelick legged out an infield single, stole second base then scored on an RBI single by Garrett Mitchell. That was the only run surrendered through three innings by October sensation Walker Buehler, who was making his first postseason appearance since finishing off the Dodgers’ 2024 World Series win. Fernando Tatis Jr. then brought life to Petco Park when he sent his second hit of the series 429-feet out to center field for a solo shot. But the Brewers did something few teams have, answering the noise of one of the best home-field advantages in the sport. Their pesky offense, which put 13 hard-hit balls into play, never went away. "When I think back to last year, I think there was an element of maybe a little bit of lack of belief that we could do it, maybe a little too much doubt," said Jake Bauers. "And I think going into this postseason, there's a different feeling around the team." There’s a tax to pay every time a reliever enters a postseason series. Hitters gain familiarity with each appearance. That might have caught up to the Padres in Wednesday’s elimination game. Brewers star left fielder Jackson Chourio roped an RBI single off Bradgley Rodriguez, who pitched in all four games of the series. Sal Frelick followed an inning later with a sacrifice fly off Jason Adam, who pitched in three of the four games, to score Jake Bauers, who reached base in each of his four plate appearances. The Padres were clearly missing star left-handed reliever Adrian Morejon, who had been nursing a sore shoulder and did not pitch after Game 1. Milwaukee starter Robert Gasser and a medley of Brewers relievers kept the Padres’ offense in check after the Tatis blast until the eighth inning provided a moment of belief, when Manny Machado sent a ball 406 feet through the San Diego night sky. He thought he got it. The crowd did, too, quiet in anticipation, ready to celebrate the game-tying blast, until Mitchell fought through a sea of Padres fans in the first row of the center-field bleachers to record the out. The Brewers cooled off baseball’s hottest team and snapped a 12-game postseason road losing streak in one of the most hostile road environments in the sport. Now, after surviving a four-game battle against the Padres, baseball’s best team will move on to face the favorites in an NLCS rematch between the Brewers and Dodgers. 4. José Ramírez Wakes Up At Right Moment Deesha Thosar: José Ramírez picked a great time to make his postseason stamp. After forgettable and hitless performances through the first two games of this ALDS, Ramirez had his fingerprints all over Game 3 as the Guardians defeated the White Sox, 9-3, and staved off elimination. He went 2-for-4 with two runs scored, two RBI and a walk at the plate. Ramirez became the 10th player to record a double, triple and stolen base in the same game in MLB postseason history. And he was excellent on both sides of the ball. Ramirez, playing in his 14th season with Cleveland, saved multiple runs from crossing the plate on a spectacular play in the dirt in the sixth inning. After right-hander Hunter Gaddis hit Sam Antonacci with the bases loaded to force in a run, White Sox third baseman Miguel Vargas ripped a liner toward short that looked like it was destined to break through the hole and into left field. But Ramirez snagged it straight off the bat for the final out of the inning. Just for good measure, he also fired a perfect throw to first, even though the inning was already over. It doesn't hurt to be sure. "It’s a great mindset from the team," Ramirez said through an interpreter after the win. "I think we did the best we could because there’s no way back. We came out to compete. There’s no tomorrow." The White Sox, who went ahead, 1-0, in the first inning, had a ton of chances to take back their lead. They put pressure on nearly every pitcher who came out of the bullpen to save Cleveland’s season. Chicago went 2-for-11 with runners in scoring position and left eight men on base. Even then, as many opportunities the South Siders had, the Guardians simply created more havoc on the basepaths. That was their plan all along. Get on base, create pressure, and force the White Sox to make near-perfect plays. Cleveland went 5-for-17 with runners in scoring position, actually piling on when they scored on Wednesday, something it had struggled to do coming into Game 3. The Guardians have Ramirez to thank for being a central figure in their critical win. "Josy, that's why he's one of the best players in the league," Guardians manager Stephen Vogt said. "He can hurt you with the bat, the legs, and the glove. He showed all that today."

articles.title: Cuándo se matriculó el primer coche en España, de qué marca era y qué distintivo provincial llevaba
articles.standfirst: Ni Madrid ni Barcelona se llevaron el mérito de tener el primer coche matriculado, que más que un coche era un cuadriciclo con una 'fuerza efectiva' de 3 caballos
articles.summary: Ni Madrid ni Barcelona se llevaron el mérito de tener el primer coche matriculado, que más que un coche era un cuadriciclo con una 'fuerza efectiva' de 2 caballos
articles.body: Hubo un tiempo en España en el que aquello de ponerle una matrícula a un coche (quizá entonces era mejor llamarlo "automóvil", para diferenciarlo mejor de los carruajes) era tan novedoso como el propio automóvil. De hecho, el primer coche matriculado en nuestro país no lo hizo en Madrid ni en Barcelona, sino en Palma de Mallorca y hace ya 126 años. La matrícula era PM-1 y el coche, un Clement con motor De Dion Bouton. Su propietario era José Sureda y Fuentes, un maquinista retirado de la Armada que vivía en Santa Catalina, en Palma. El 31 de octubre de 1900 quedó registrado como el primer automóvil del archivo histórico de matriculaciones español. Pero hay que hacer una pequeña precisión porque la historia del coche en España había empezado en realidad antes. El 8 de abril de 1897 había desembarcado en Palma un Clement Bayard adquirido en París por el industrial Vicente Juan Ribas. De hecho, se dice que este último fue el primer automóvil que llegó a Mallorca y uno de los primeros que pudieron contemplarse en nuestro país. Pero aquel coche nunca llegó a matricularse porque el invento de las matrículas todavía no había llegado a nuestro país. Su propietario terminó encerrándolo en una cochera de su finca de Son Puig de sa Vileta, donde se dice que todavía lo conservan sus herederos, lo que no se ha podido confirmar. El PM-1 era bastante muy, muy modesto comparado con lo que hoy entendemos por un coche. La documentación de Tráfico lo identifica como un cuadriciclo Clement con motor De Dion Bouton de unos 3 CV, 130 kilos de peso y ruedas de 65 centímetros de diámetro. Así que, más que nada, se planteaba como una alternativa a un pequeño carruaje de caballos. Su velocidad máxima rondaba los 30 km/h y en las subidas se quedaba en unos 15 km/h, según unas de declaraciones que hizo Juan Vidal Sureda, sobrino del propietario, allá por 1969. ¿Y cuánto costaba aquel pequeño Clement? No se sabe con exactitud, pero el sobrino de José Sureda habló en su momento de que su tío había pagado 3.000 pesetas al representante en España de los fabricantes franceses Clement De Dion Bouton. Para hacerse una idea de lo que significaban 3.000 pesetas hay que ponerlas en relación con los salarios de la época. No existía entonces un estudio que estableciera un salario medio nacional comparable al que manejamos hoy, y las diferencias entre oficios y regiones eran por lo visto enormes. A comienzos del siglo XX un agricultor cobrar alrededor de 1 o 1,50 pesetas al día, mientras que en determinados oficios industriales los salarios llegaban a 4 pesetas. Pero sí se sabe que, por ejemplo, en 1909 el salario medio anual de un minero era de 780 pesetas. Tomando esa cifra como referencia, aquellas 3.000 pesetas equivaldrían a casi cuatro años de sueldo íntegro. Y eso suponiendo que el trabajador pudiera dedicar hasta la última peseta a comprar el coche. ¿Y qué ocurrió con aquel primer coche? Aquí la historia del PM-1 se vuelve mucho más oscura. Sabemos que perteneció a José Sureda y que su sobrino todavía recordaba detalles del coche casi 70 años después de ser matriculado. Pero nada se sabe de lo que pasó con aquel coche. El que sí se conserva en España, y todavía es más antiguo aunque no fuera el primero en ser matriculado, es es un Delahaye Tipo 1 de 1899 que pertenece a la colección de la Fundación RACE y que actualmente se encuentra en el Museo de Historia de la Automoción de Salamanca. Como imaginarás, este Delahaye es una artilugio mucho más cercano a un carruaje que a lo que entendemos por un coche. De hecho, carece incluso de volante, ya que para dirigirlo se utilizaban una palanca cuya forma le valió el curioso nombre de "cola de vaca". Su propietario, el Conde del Valle, protagonizó además una de las primeras hazañas del automovilismo español al coronar con él el puerto de Guadarrama y, décadas después, aquel mismo coche participó en la inauguración del túnel de Guadarrama en 1963.

articles.title: Así es Victoria Vilchez, la sorpresa argentina del Mundial y 358 del ránking: "La comparan con Claudia Fernández"
articles.standfirst: La jugadora albiceleste de 16 años fue la novedad de la lista para la cita de Doha. Entrenadores y compañeras la analizan en MARCA Pádel
articles.summary: La jugadora albiceleste de 16 años fue la novedad de la lista para la cita de Doha. Entrenadores y compañeras la analizan en MARCA Pádel
articles.body: Con solo 16 años, Victoria Vilchez está a punto de vivir uno de esos momentos que pueden marcar para siempre una carrera deportiva. La joven argentina, actualmente número 358 del ránking FIP, debutará con la selección absoluta femenina de Argentina en una cita mundialista. Un salto mayúsculo para una jugadora que todavía compite en la categoría júnior, pero que lleva tiempo llamando a la puerta de la élite con una personalidad en pista impropia de su edad. Vilchez recibió la noticia visiblemente emocionada y, entre lágrimas, reconoce que todavía no termina de creérselo: “Estoy súper contenta con esta noticia. No lo puedo creer, la verdad. Estoy muy emocionada, no caigo en esto, en estar convocada para jugar entre las mejores del mundo. La verdad que era un sueño para mí y poder estar ahora es increíble”. A sus 16 años le toca vivir el sueño que, hasta hace no tanto, parecía demasiado grande para imaginarlo. Su historia con el pádel comenzó casi por casualidad. Tenía apenas ocho años cuando acompañó a sus padres a un partido y quedó enganchada a un deporte que terminaría convirtiéndose en su profesión. A los 11 disputó su primer torneo y poco después comenzó a competir en la liga de menores en Argentina. Con 13 años ganó todos los selectivos de Menores y en 2023 formó parte del equipo argentino que conquistó la medalla de plata en el Mundial de Menores, compartiendo generación con jugadoras que hoy ya están asentadas en la élite, como Claudia Jensen. En 2025, además, terminó como número uno del ránking de menores en su país. Pero el crecimiento de Vilchez no se ha detenido al abandonar la etapa formativa. Su primera experiencia con la albiceleste absoluta llegó en los Juegos Panamericanos de 2025, celebrados en Santiago de Chile. Allí compartió pista con Martina Fassio y respondió a la confianza ganando su punto en la final. “Me sorprendió mucho su madurez en la pista”, recuerda Fassio sobre aquella primera experiencia. Un año después, Vilchez ya sabe también lo que significa competir en Premier Padel: debutó en el Buenos Aires P1 y continúa acumulando experiencias frente a jugadoras de máximo nivel. La temporada 2026 ha añadido otro capítulo a una progresión que parece no tener techo. Vilchez se colgó la medalla de oro en los Juegos Suramericanos y ahora recibe una nueva oportunidad con la selección absoluta. Para Rodri Ovide, seleccionador de Argentina, no hay lugar para dudas: “Vicky llega a la convocatoria para el Mundial por méritos propios”. Una frase que resume perfectamente el camino de una jugadora que, pese a su juventud y a ocupar todavía el puesto 358 del ranking mundial, se ha ganado un lugar entre las mejores de su país Su nombre empieza, además, a despertar comparaciones. En Argentina hay quien encuentra similitudes con alguna jugadora española, “Aquí en Argentina la comparan mucho con Claudia Fernández. Tiene un estilo de juego similar, se parece incluso en los gestos”, apunta su entrenador Maxi Yze. Y si algo parece tener claro el entorno de la selección es que Vilchez representa una apuesta de futuro. Gaby Reca, seleccionador argentino, lo explica así: “Es una chica con mucha proyección y, como siempre decimos, en el tema de las mujeres estamos tratando de preparar un equipo futuro porque España es un equipazo. Estamos trabajando en el equipo femenino para poder ser competitivos en un par de mundiales”. Su juventud no está reñida con una identidad de juego cada vez más definida. Ceci Reiter, referente del pádel argentino y seleccionadora de menores, la describe como “una jugadora consistente, regular y con gran capacidad de desborde”. Un perfil ofensivo y con personalidad que ayuda a entender por qué, con apenas 16 años, Vilchez ya ha conseguido hacerse un hueco entre las mayores. Ahora, Vilchez tendrá la oportunidad de convertir toda esa proyección en una primera experiencia mundialista con la absoluta. Será una de las jugadoras más jóvenes del torneo y, probablemente, una de las grandes historias a seguir dentro del equipo argentino. Con 16 años, el ranking 358 del mundo y una personalidad que ya sorprende a quienes han compartido pista con ella, Vicky Vilchez llega a su primer Mundial no como una invitada, sino como una jugadora que se lo ha ganado.

articles.title: High drama at Asian Games send-off as para-shooters allege corruption, protest selection process
articles.summary: High drama unfolded on Thursday at the send-off ceremony for the Indian contingent headed to the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games, with several para-shooters
articles.body: High drama unfolded on Thursday at the send-off ceremony for the Indian contingent headed to the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Para Games, with several para-shooters protesting outside the venue and alleging corruption and manipulation in the selection process.The protesters were met by senior Paralympic Committee of India (PCI) officials, including president Devendra Jhajharia, who tried to persuade them to call off the demonstration, news agency PTI reported. The shooters, however, continued their protest, raising slogans before explaining their grievances.The PCI rejected the allegations, saying the team for the Aichi-Nagoya Para-Asian Games, scheduled from October 18 to 24, was selected transparently, entirely on merit and according to the prescribed criteria.Among those leading the protest were para-shooters Sandeep Kumar and Akash, who questioned their exclusion from the contingent despite their rankings and performances.Sandeep is ranked third in Asia, while Akash is the top-ranked shooter on the continent. They also questioned the inclusion of Rudransh Khandelwal, who they said is ranked 14th in Asia.The protest later moved to the porch area of the venue where the send-off ceremony was scheduled to take place. India head coach Satyanarayana and Jhajharia spoke to the athletes and asked them to end the protest, but the shooters remained firm.Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya attended the ceremony while the protest was still underway.Akash alleged that his credentials were overlooked because he had not named shooting coach Jai Prakash Nautiyal as his coach."That is why he cut my name. I have been here for two months. He keeps saying that we are doing your work. Every day, he says that we are doing your work, but he is not doing anything," Akash alleged.Sandeep, a P4 50m free pistol SH1 shooter, said he did not receive any assurance from Jhajharia even after showing documents supporting his case.Asked what Jhajharia had told him, Sandeep said, "Nothing.""We showed the papers to Jhajharia ji and other PCI officials. Rahul Swami, Vivek Saini, who is a para-shooter and has not played a single shooting match, has been made an expert. He misguides people," Sandeep alleged, as quoted by PTI.He also made allegations against Nautiyal, claiming that the coach sought a 20 per cent commission from government cash awards in return for helping athletes secure selection.Sandeep also questioned why the athletes were being asked to end their protest at the last moment, saying they had been raising their concerns for several days."They said that the Asian Games send-off ceremony is today's programme. Now they are telling us not to hold this protest. They said, till 2:30 pm, 'we will send your name in the list'. So how will they send our names now, when we have been sending them for so many days?” he said.Akash claimed that the sports ministry's guidelines required the top six athletes to be considered for selection and alleged that the criteria had not been followed."We will provide you with the documents. They (those selected) have not played internationally. And in the national selection trial that has taken place, the scores are being changed," Akash alleged."There are people in para shooting who cannot even become members, yet they have been made officials. We want justice," he added.The shooters had submitted a representation to the Director General of the Sports Authority of India (SAI) on Wednesday, seeking an urgent, high-level independent inquiry into what they described as "illicit monetary extortion", "brazen corruption" and violation of the ministry's guidelines by PCI officials and its Shooting Technical Committee (STC).Among their most serious allegations was that athletes were being pressured to pay a 20 per cent commission from government cash awards as a condition for selection. articles.title: ¡Un hincha de los Yankees intercepta un posible home run que hubiera evitado la eliminación de su equipo!
articles.standfirst: Atrapó la pelota en pleno vuelo cuando aún no había salido del campo y acabó expulsado del estadio por su imprudencia
articles.summary: Atrapó la pelota en pleno vuelo cuando aún no había salido del campo y acabó expulsado del estadio por su imprudencia
articles.body: ¿Se imaginan que en el fútbol los espectadores estuvieran tan cerca del terreno de juego que pudieran tocar la pelota junto a la banda o la línea de fondo? Suena a ciencia ficción pero hay un deporte donde estas cosas pasan. No con frecuencia, cierto, pero a veces de forma determinante, como pasó anoche en el Yankee Stadium de Nueva York. Les ponemos en contexto. Los 'Bombarderos del Bronx' recibían a los Tampa Bay Rays en el tercer partido de su Serie Divisional, con ventaja para el equipo de Florida por 2-0, a un solo triunfo de la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana. Estamos en la parte baja de la sexta entrada y Tampa Bay gana por 4-2 cuando Anthony Volpe conecta un posible home run que hubiera empatado el partido, pues otro jugador de los New York Yankees está en la segunda base, sumando esa carrera a la suya propia. La pelota vuela hasta el muro y justo cuando Víctor Mesa Jr., 'outfielder' de los Rays, intenta atraparla, un aficionado de los Yankees mete la mano por encima del muro y atrapa la pelota, desatando las protestas del jugador cubano. El Yanke Stadium estalla de alegría pero los árbitros revisan la jugada en el Replay Review (videoarbitraje de la Major League Baseball) y anulan el home run. Más tarde, en un comunicado, la MLB afirmaría haber "dilucidado de manera definitiva que el espectador interfirió con la pelota sobre el terreno de juego" tras analizar "todos los ángulos relevantes". “La pelota no habría salido del terreno de juego ni habría sido atrapada. La decisión se revoca, hubo interferencia de un espectador y no fue home run”, declaró la liga en ese comunicado. “Además, el árbitro de repetición anotó una carrera y colocó al bateador-corredor en segunda base”. Dicho de otro modo, los árbitros interpretaron que Mesa Jr. quizás no hubiera atrapado la pelota en pleno vuelo pero ésta no hubiera sobrepasado el muro, dándole la oportunidad de evitar la segunda carrera. Los Yankees por tanto sumaron una carrera y siguieron perdiendo aunque por 4-3, marcador que no se movería en las tras entradas restantes, lo que conllevó la eliminación del equipo neoyorquino y el pase de los Rays a la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana. Finalmente, el aficionado fue expulsado del estadio junto a un amigo, mientras eran escoltados por un miembro uniformado del Departamento de Policía de Nueva York y lo que parecían ser varios miembros del personal de seguridad del Yankee Stadium.

articles.title: Malik Nabers spoke to John Harbaugh about "trying to give me the ball down the field"
articles.summary: Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had his most productive day of the season in last Sunday's win over the Cardinals, but he said on Wednesday that he feels "...
articles.body:
Giants wide receiver Malik Nabers had his most productive day of the season in last Sunday's win over the Cardinals, but he said on Wednesday that he feels "like that was a basic game" rather than a breakthrough as he continues working his way back from last season's torn ACL.

Nabers caught six passes for 112 yards and a touchdown that he followed up by letting head coach John Harbaugh know that he wanted the team to keep feeding him the ball. That didn't happen in the second half as Nabers only had one catch in the final 30 minutes and he explained why he was animated in discussions with the sideline in those moments.

"I felt like I didn't get targeted much after halftime," Nabers said, via a transcript from the team. "So, that was just a thing. It's just – I felt like creating explosives down the field was just helping us get in a better position to score touchdowns. Some of those plays didn't come my way, so just trying to figure out why."

Nabers revisited the issue with Harbaugh after the game and shared that the conversation was about the kinds of adjustments that the team is making during halftime.

"Just also trying to give me the ball down the field to create some of those opportunities for us to gain more points," Nabers said. "It felt like during the first half when we did that, it kind of led into the right direction with scoring touchdowns in the red zone. And just — after that, we just couldn't get going. So, I felt like the offense was needing a spark and I wanted to be that spark, so I was just trying to figure out what was going on, and what was the thought process on going into after halftime and coming out, what was the talk that he had with the coaches on implementing things down the field — we had a talk about it."

Nabers didn't practice on Wednesday and is listed with a knee he said was "a little bit more sore" than usual. He said that they'll see how things go the rest of the week when asked if it could impact his availability against the Commanders this Sunday and that will have to play out before we find out if the Giants will be feeding their top wideout the ball more often.

articles.title: ‘Those Were Not Sam Darnold Problems’: Kevin O’Connell Takes Blame for Vikings’ Two Biggest Losses
articles.summary: The Minnesota Vikings have moved on from Sam Darnold, however, head coach Kevin O’Connell clearly has not forgotten how his final season with the Vikings end...
articles.body:
The Minnesota Vikings have moved on from Sam Darnold , however, head coach Kevin O'Connell clearly has not forgotten how his final season with the Vikings ended. Two painful losses in 2024 became easy targets for quarterback blame, especially after Darnold struggled in both games.

Now, O'Connell is pushing back on that narrative. With the Vikings sitting at 4-0 in 2026, Connell offered a striking admission about those losses and took responsibility for what went wrong.

Kevin O'Connell Takes Responsibility for Sam Darnold's Vikings Losses

Connell made the comments on October 7, 2026, while discussing the Vikings' QB situation and the way Darnold was viewed after the 2024 season. Rather than defend every decision from that period, he put the responsibility squarely on himself and the organization.

"Everybody wanted to put, whether it was the win for 1 seed game against Detroit, or the playoff game against LA, those were not Sam Darnold problems, those were Minnesota Vikings problems… everybody wanted to pin those games on Sam, which I thought was unfair. If anything it should kinda be put on me."

That is a notable change in tone compared with how those games were discussed at the time. Darnold became the obvious target after the Vikings lost to the Detroit Lions in Week 18 and then fell to the Los Angeles Rams in the playoffs. The quarterback's mistakes were highly visible; however, the HC now believes the failures went much deeper than one position.

And there is plenty of context behind that admission . O'Connell previously argued that organizations c an fail young quarterbacks before quarterbacks fail organizations. That belief has followed him throughout the J.J. McCarthy saga, particularly after the Vikings traded the former No. 10 overall pick to the Giants on October 5.

McCarthy's departure has put O'Connell under another layer of scrutiny. Minnesota helped build the situation around the quarterback, and the head coach acknowledged Monday that sometimes things simply do not develop as planned.

That makes his latest comments even more interesting. O'Connell is not running from responsibility n ow, just as he did not completely distance himself from the decision to draft McCarthy.

The Vikings have still managed to start 4-0 despite major questions on offense. Their passing game has struggled, and injuries have complicated the quarterback picture, but the 41-year-old has shifted his focus toward winning rather than chasing impressive numbers.

That philosophy may be the biggest takeaway. O'Connell knows some decisions have not worked; however, instead of pinning the failures on the quarterback, he is willing to own his share.

articles.title: DeChambeau Contract Uncertainty Grows After Rahm Exit
articles.summary: Bryson DeChambeau's future hangs in the balance as Jon Rahm leaves LIV Golf, with legal clarity sought on contracts and over $100 million still owed.
articles.body:
The landscape of professional golf changed again on Wednesday. Jon Rahm confirmed he will not play in LIV Golf's future. This decision leaves the breakaway league without one of its biggest stars. It puts massive pressure on Bryson DeChambeau.

The American is now arguably the most important name the league must keep. His current contract expires at the end of 2026, but he remains legally tied to the tour. Lawyers for DeChambeau and several other players are now asking for answers. They want to know if their deals are still valid. The situation is messy, and the clock is ticking fast.

The latest update came from Front Office Sports' David Rumsey, who reported that lawyers representing DeChambeau, Cam Smith, Ben An, Marc Leishman, Cameron Tringale, Matthew Wolff and Harold Varner III have all sought further clarity over their contracts. This legal push happened right after Sergio Garcia successfully terminated his own deal.

Garcia is now a free agent because he worried about how his LIV status hurt his other opportunities. LIV has the right to reject certain contracts, but the process takes time. On Wednesday, league lawyers could not give a definite answer. The matter goes back to court on October 14.

Rahm's exit highlights the financial trouble the league faces. He joined in late 2023 for a blockbuster $350m move. He won three straight titles and earned another $100 million in prize money. But the money stopped coming when Saudi funding vanished. According to MARCA , "it is believed that Rahm is owed more than $100 million."

Awful Announcing reported that his lawyer told the US Bankruptcy Court the new terms were "unacceptable to him." The league is trying to survive as a leaner tour without billions in government cash. This leaves players like DeChambeau in a tough spot. They are waiting to see if the league can even pay them.

Bryson DeChambeau is in a unique position. He is the face of the power game and the most famous remaining star. If he leaves, the league loses its main selling point. The uncertainty is dangerous for his career. He cannot plan his schedule or find new sponsors without knowing where he stands.

The court hearing on Wednesday showed that players are ready to walk away if they have to. Rahm's lawyer said, "I don't really know how things will play out with the DP World Tour regarding LIV 2.0." He added, "We'll have to wait and see. That doesn't mean I won't go or that I'll definitely stay with LIV. I do what I believe is best for myself, my family and my team."

This quote shows that even the biggest stars are not sure what comes next. DeChambeau has not said he is leaving, but his legal team is asking hard questions. The court date on October 14 is the next big step. If the league cannot pay the millions it owes, players will have little reason to stay. The golf world watches closely to see if DeChambeau follows Rahm or stays to fight for a share of the remaining pie.

Everyone waits for the next legal move. The court hearing is set for October 14. This is when lawyers will try to get a clear answer on the contracts. Until then, the future remains unclear for DeChambeau and the others. The league must show it can survive without the billions it once had. The next few weeks will decide if LIV Golf 2.0 is real or just a dream.

articles.title: Have Yankees gone all in? ‘It’s tough to say,’ Aaron Judge says after ALDS exit
articles.summary: As the Rays celebrated on the field at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday night, a few Yankees lingered in the dugout and watched their rival’s joy in pain. Among t...
articles.body:
As the Rays celebrated on the field at Yankee Stadium on Wednesday night, a few Yankees lingered in the dugout and watched their rival's joy in pain.

Among them were Aaron Judge and George Lombard Jr. The latter seemed distraught over the fact that his first postseason had just ended with a sweep in the ALDS . Still wearing his pinstripes, the rookie Lombard rested his head in his folded arms on the dugout railing.

Judge, meanwhile, stared off at the Rays, hoodie up and a jacket on. Sidelined by a calf strain suffered in mid-September, he never suited up for the Yankees this October.

"It definitely hurts," Judge said. "You want to be out there."

Alas, Judge never got his wish. Now, the next time he sets foot on a field, the Yankees are sure to have a new-look roster, as Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trent Grisham, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Paul Goldschmidt are among the team's free agents. The first two are change of scenery candidates, even though they expressed a desire to return on Wednesday.

Speaking more generally, second base, third base, center field, the bullpen and catcher — a right-handed hitting one is needed — are among the Yankees' question marks as another offseason begins with the extension of a championship drought that has reached 17 years.

Asked how Brian Cashman and Hal Steinbrenner should react to the team's latest letdown, Judge replied, "We're the Yankees. I feel like they should go all in and do what they need to do. If we got holes, it's finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you gotta go out there and get it. That's why I signed back here to play with the Yankees, to fight for a championship every single year. We go all in. That's what I do every offseason: get ready to give this team and the city everything I got. So I expect them to do the same."

The captain's response begged a follow-up: does he believe the organization has gone all in enough during his 11-year, ringless tenure?

A pause followed. Then an answer that didn't dispel the notion.

"It's tough to say," Judge said. "I want to trade for everybody and sign everybody every single year, but I know that's not realistic. So they give us a winning team every single year, but that's not good enough here in New York. We're the Yankees. You gotta go out there and expect championships and go all in every year, so I'm excited to see what they do."

Judge's comments came after a rinse and repeat season.

After losing the American League East and then the ALDS to the Blue Jays in 2025, the Yankees took a so-called "run it back" approach last offseason and retained a largely similar roster.

This year, they lost the division to the Rays while battling numerous injuries — Judge also missed 99 days with a fractured rib — and were swept by Tampa Bay in the ALDS. The Rays did so despite ranking 27th with a projected luxury tax payroll of $112.9 million, per Cot's Contracts.

The Yankees ranked third with a $341.8 million payroll.

While Judge endorsed the team's "run it back" tactic back in spring training, he didn't seem eager to try it again as the Yankees packed up their clubhouse on Wednesday.

"The toughest thing is each year, besides us, every other team gets better," Judge said. "Every other team's adding new players, getting new coaches, new philosophies, things they can do to improve their team. So it's not like, 'Hey, we're just going to run it back and we'll be in the postseason.'

"We'll start right back here and we'll fix the slate. You gotta start back at 0-0 and work through the grind again against tougher opponents. It's going to be a grind, but it's just about trying to be 1% better than those guys and trying to get 1% better every day in the offseason. Hopefully, we show up and rewrite the script."

Even if the Yankees meet Judge's definition of "all out" this offseason — it's unclear what he wants them to do, or what he wanted them to do differently — the impending free agent class is limited. Two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal will be the top prize available, but the Yankees don't necessarily need rotation help. Chisholm could be the most talented position player available after a disappointing year — that's how weak this class is — and he may have worn out his welcome in the Bronx during a down season.

Also complicating matters this winter will be the threat of a lockout, as the Collective Bargaining Agreement expires on Dec. 1. It's possible a work stoppage will take another chunk of a season away from Judge.

Now 34, he is running out of time to win a ring. So it's understandable that he didn't waste time nudging the Yankees to make sufficient additions after Wednesday's ALDS exit.

But he also sent a message to those already in the clubhouse before embarking on another premature offseason.

"There's a standard to winning a championship," said Judge, still searching for his first. "It's black and white. There's no gray area. It's every day you show up to work. Every little thing you do is 'Are you working toward a championship or you're not?' So I think that's the biggest thing, is just everybody in the room understanding you gotta bring it every single day, especially here in New York. There's no days off, and it just comes down to the little things and just preparing every single day like you're preparing for a championship game."
authors: Gary Phillips, New York Daily News

articles.title: Jeanie Buss Accused of Self-Interest as Family Fights to Sell $2.2B Lakers Stake
articles.summary: A major fight within the Buss family is growing over the future of the Los Angeles Lakers. Some family members say Jeanie Buss does not have the legal power...
articles.body:
A major fight within the Buss family is growing over the future of the Los Angeles Lakers. Some family members say Jeanie Buss does not have the legal power to stop them from selling their minority stakes in the team.

They claim her effort to block a possible sale is driven by personal interests, not the Lakers' legacy. With $2.2 billion at stake, the dispute could reshape who controls the franchise and deepen divisions within the family.

Billion-dollar stake sale tests Jeanie Buss's control of Lakers

Jeanie Buss's siblings are challenging her legal effort to prevent them from selling their ownership interests in the Lakers. The dispute centers on whether the family trust gives Jeanie authority to block a transaction involving minority shares. The legal challenge does not mean a sale has been completed, and the $2.2 billion figure describes the possible value connected to the proposed deal.

"Jeanie Buss's family members say she has no right to stop them from selling their ownership of the Lakers, which could make them $2.2B through the sale," the report stated . Those statements are the siblings' position in the dispute, not a final court finding.

The conflict dates back to Dr. Jerry Buss's 1979 purchase of the Lakers and the family trust created after his death in 2013. Jeanie became the franchise's controlling owner and governor, and her siblings retained interests in the family structure. Earlier disagreements involving Jim Buss and Johnny Buss established a history of internal power struggles. The case also combines that history with a possible ownership transaction worth billions.

Root of family resistance over potential Lakers sale

The Lakers' ownership structure was built to keep control within the Buss family after Jerry Buss died. Jeanie represents the franchise, but relatives say their trust interests carry separate economic rights. Any sale, therefore, raises questions about trust, language, governance, and the limits of Jeanie's role.

At the center is the potential $2.2 billion return for the siblings. They argue Jeanie's petition is "driven by her own personal desire to preserve" her leadership roles with the Lakers, according to the ownership report . The claim remains disputed , and the court must determine how the trust rules apply to a possible sale. The legal outcome will ultimately define the franchise's governance moving forward.

A sale to outside investors could alter the voting balance and affect board decisions, financing, and the relationship between Jeanie's role and shareholders' rights. The court's reading of trust documents may shape the Lakers' ownership chapter.

articles.summary: Winning a conference title isn’t any easy accomplishment. Edgewood’s volleyball team claimed its third straight Chagrin Valley Conference Lake Division title...
articles.body:
Winning a conference title isn't any easy accomplishment.

Edgewood's volleyball team claimed its third straight Chagrin Valley Conference Lake Division title with a 25-19, 25-12, 25-20 win over Lakeside Monday night.

The Warriors then defeated North 25-16, 21-25, 25-16, 25-14 Tuesday night, and are 11-0 in the conference, 16-2 overall.

"It feels amazing to be here again — three straight CVC titles — and I'm so proud of all we've accomplished so far. We've only dropped eight sets so far on the year overall, and the girls are working hard."

After hosting Saint John for Senior Night Monday, Edgewood's last conference match is Tuesday at home against Geneva, which is also concludes the regular season.

In the win over the Dragons, Summer Matthews scored 14 points and notched 27 assists.

At the net, Faith Vencill recorded 17 kills, three blocks and 10 digs.

Payton Woodring, Jerzi Patton and Antoria Taylor also collected three blocks apiece.

Vencill had 26 kills and 21 digs; Matthews, 42 assists and three aces; Patton, 13 points; Woodring, three aces and Taylor, nine blocks, against the Rangers.

"We were able to handle ourselves in serve receive as they tend to be aggressive in serving and have the leading ace server in the county, as well as state-wise in [Gabby] Kaplan," coach Vencill said. "We knew we had to limit our errors, and wanted to control tempo."

Vencill said the team is doing well with getting the offense going on free-ball opportunities, and being aggressive with the ball.

"We have also started being more aggressive on the service line," she said.

But she also realizes there's more work that needs to be done as the regular season winds down.

"The things we know we need to get better at is being able to run offense consistently right out of serve receive," Vencill said. "It's something we practice toward, and need to see happen in games more often."

The Warriors are scheduled to participate in the Division IV postseason tournament. Last season, Edgewood lost in a district final match, after reaching the regional tournament two seasons ago.

"Our main focus will be trusting offense in tight games going into the tournament," Vencill said. "These will be closer games, and remaining focused on the point at hand. Tournament play will be tough as many great teams, and we need to handle the point at hand, and not allow errors to cost us."

articles.title: Hamilton says racing in the rain is not the same as caution reigns
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton feels the caution of Formula One bosses and its younger drivers has taken away some of the sport’s “seat of your pants” wet-weather driving. T...
articles.body:
Lewis Hamilton feels the caution of Formula One bosses and its younger drivers has taken away some of the sport's "seat of your pants" wet-weather driving.

The seven-time world champion was speaking in response to last weekend's shambolic scenes in Malaysia, which saw drivers effectively unable to power their vehicles in the wet conditions.

The Bahrain Grand Prix held at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia was overshadowed as F1 bosses had to abandon the start when a number of drivers, including Max Verstappen and Hamilton, were struck by gremlins – directly linked to the controversial 50-50 split between combustion and battery power – on the formation lap.

The grid eventually limped back to the pit lane and the race got under way after a 53-minute delay. It later emerged that new software had to be downloaded to the cars.

As a result of the painstaking delay, the track was significantly drier than it was at the scheduled start time – with cars deployed on a mixture of intermediate and slick tyres.

Full-wet tyres are seldom used in modern F1 and Hamilton was asked whether – aside from the unprecedented software glitch – a more conservative pattern has developed when it comes to racing in the rain.

"Wet-weather races aren't the same as we used to have, for sure," Hamilton said in Singapore ahead of this weekend's race.

"I've had great races, in 2008 in the rain, and ultimately back then we had more testing and we did have better tyres for the rain. I love wet racing more than anything else.

"I do think the guys running the show are far more cautious but then again the young drivers coming in are more and more cautious.

"Us old-school drivers are like 'let's get racing', and more of the youngsters are like 'let's not race'. So they're (the FIA) getting two different bits of information, and they are super cautious as well.

"That's where I'm like 'let's get going'. That's where we really get to test ourselves. Is it more risky? Absolutely."

Hamilton has made a reputation as an outstanding wet-weather driver, highlighted by his brilliant 2008 win at Silverstone, and again showed his prowess to fight back to third having dropped to 18th after mistakenly starting on slick tyres.

"When I was out on the slick tyre, it was the trickiest conditions," Hamilton added.

"It was wet, I was on slicks, but I love that challenge. And that's what racing is, where you have to drive by the seat of the pants, and that's really where you can make the difference."

Cars will receive a software update in a bid prevent a re-run of the embarrassing scenes in Malaysia.

Having pledged a full investigation, governing body the FIA revealed on Thursday that a "software bug" was at fault and plans updates across the coming races should similar conditions be faced.

"The review concluded that some cars running on low engine RPM in certain circuit sectors where a 250kW power reduction was applied experienced a loss of power beyond the original intent and that could not be recovered in those sectors," an FIA statement read.

"As a result, the configuration established for the Sepang event will be reinstated for the Singapore Grand Prix should similar weather conditions be expected. Additionally, a further update to the wet weather software will be released for the United States Grand Prix on October 25."

Verstappen, who has been the fiercest critic of the 2026 regulations, hopes for a far simpler set-up when the next regulations are devised.

He said: "The problem is it is very complex, I just hope the next rule set is easier. You should be able to go out, have a brake pedal and throttle pedal and that is what is deciding the lap time."

articles.title: Russell reflects on misfortune and admits ‘it’s tough to take’
articles.summary: George Russell believes misfortune has prevented him from being able to put Formula One champion-in-waiting Kimi Antonelli under significant title pressure....
articles.body:
George Russell believes misfortune has prevented him from being able to put Formula One champion-in-waiting Kimi Antonelli under significant title pressure.

Russell's devastating late engine failure in Malaysia last weekend leaves him 84 points behind Antonelli with only seven scheduled races, and a possible 183 points, remaining.

It means the 20-year-old Italian is almost certain to lift his maiden world championship after Russell was again undone by reliability issues. He also retired from the Canadian Grand Prix in May and has been beset by ill-fortune throughout the season.

To compound Russell's problems, he has had to take a new power unit this weekend and so will start at the rear of the grid and he confirmed he is set to need another before the end of the season – which will incur another penalty.

The 28-year-old again confessed that Antonelli, who passed his Mercedes team-mate on track in Malaysia, has showed better performance throughout the season but believes in normal circumstances he would still be in the fight.

"The guy who's performed the best is the guy who's leading the championship," Russell said ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

"If you add up the numbers and the points, I still think I'd be very much in the game in an ordinary season. I still think I'd be on the back foot, but in the game for it to flip very quick.

"When you add up the points from this season that have been lost, you know, I've probably had more failures this year than I've had in the three seasons put together.

"Of course, it's tough to take. If I'm being 100% fair with myself, as I've said before, the performance this season hasn't been strong enough. And it probably would have affected me more if these results have… like, who knows if I'd have still been in the fight or not, in a more normal circumstance.

"But obviously the pressure and the momentum, every setback has an impact on that momentum.

"It's been pretty incredible how things have panned out this year. But you've just got to focus on what you can control."

Russell will switch back to the car with which he won the Azerbaijan Grand Prix a fortnight ago while Antonelli will run Mercedes' Malaysia upgrade – after a weekend which boss Toto Wolff labelled their "worst" of the season.

articles.title: Matt Campbell nearly became USC football coach five years ago
articles.summary: In November of 2021, Matt Campbell was rumored to be USC's next coach. Now he faces Lincoln Riley with Riley on the hot seat. It's an amazing story
articles.body:
As USC football prepares to play Penn State, we are reminded that the man who will coach against Lincoln Riley this Saturday almost became the Trojans ' head coach. Matt Campbell versus USC is one of the many amazing storylines attached to this Week 6 clash in Happy Valley.

It was Thanksgiving Friday of 2021. Iowa State played TCU on a Friday. Because coaches can't interview for other open jobs until their 12-game regular seasons end, Matt Campbell had a leg up on the rest of the field because his 12th and final game of the 2021 regular season was on a Friday. Lincoln Riley's 12th regular season game was on Saturday that weekend. Moreover, if Riley's Oklahoma Sooners defeated Oklahoma State on that Saturday night, the Sooners would have advanced to the Big 12 Championship Game, preventing Riley from interviewing with USC or anyone else.

On that Friday, Matt Campbell was viewed as the man with the inside track to the USC head coaching job. He was the person most prominently and regularly attached to the coaching carousel rumor mill and the industry chatter behind the scenes. Being able to finish his game Friday gave him the opportunity to interview on Saturday morning or at lunchtime while his colleagues, including Riley, couldn't do anything.

However, as we now know, USC's Brandon Sosna - the right-hand man to then-athletic director Mike Bohn - had carved out a line of communication with Riley's representation. The hope from USC's end was that Oklahoma would lose to Oklahoma State so that direct communication with Riley could take place right after the Sooners played the Cowboys. OU did lose to Oklahoma State. Sosna and Bohn had their chance. They pounced. The rest is history.

Matt Campbell never did become USC's next head coach. Now he coaches against USC in the Big Ten as Penn State's new boss. Campbell and Riley coached against each other often in the Big 12. Now they carry their coaching clash to the Big Ten. It is wild these two coaches are meeting under these circumstances, with Riley's USC tenure hanging in the balance as an added plot point in Happy Valley on Saturday.

You couldn't make up any of this stuff if you tried.
